  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent services
  to enhance the quality of life for our entire community.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
You may speak up to 5 minutes on Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with another
person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City Council
may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted up to 24
hours before the meeting via email to mpclerk@montereypark.ca.gov.

Per the Americans with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting,
please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359 for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting.
Council Chambers are wheelchair accessible.

4-A.  ADOPTION OF A RESOLUTION ADDING NEW USER FEES AND CHARGES RELATING TO

4-B.  THE CITY IS REQUIRED TO CONDUCT A PUBLIC HEARING TO CONSIDER
  ASSESSMENTS FOR THE CITYWIDE MAINTENANCE DISTRICT NO. 93-1 FOR FISCAL
  YEAR 2023-24 PURSUANT TO STREETS AND HIGHWAYS CODE §§ 22500, ET SEQ.
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Opening the public hearing and receive documentary and testimonial evidence;
  (2) Closing the public hearing and adopt a Resolution authorizing the Levy and Collection of
  Assessments for Fiscal Year 2023-24 in Citywide Maintenance District No. 93-1 pursuant

  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  The proposed action is exempt from review under the California Environmental Quality Act (Cal.
  Pub. Res. Code §§ 21000, et seq.; “CEQA”) and CEQA Guidelines (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 14, §§
  15000, et seq.) because it establishes, modifies, structures, restructures, and approves rates
  and charges for meeting operating expenses; purchasing supplies, equipment, and materials;
  meeting financial requirements; and obtaining funds for capital projects needed to maintain

4-C.  A CONTINUED PUBLIC HEARING TO CONSIDER INTRODUCTION AND FIRST READING
  OF ZONING CODE AMENDMENT NO. 23-01(ZCA-23-01), AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE
  MONTEREY PARK MUNICIPAL CODE, CHAPTER 21.18, ENTITLED “AFFORDABLE
  HOUSING INCENTIVES – DENSITY BONUS” TO IMPLEMENT THE MONTEREY PARK
  HOUSING ELEMENT
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Opening the continued public hearing and taking testimonial and documentary evidence;
  (2) After closing the public hearing and considering the evidence submitted during that public
  hearing, introduce and waive first reading of Ordinance No. _____ amending Chapter
  21.18 (Affordable Housing Incentives – Density Bonus) to Monterey Park Municipal Code
  Title 21 (Zoning) to implement the Monterey Park Housing Element; and
  (3) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  The proposed Ordinance is exempt from additional environmental review under the California
  Environmental Quality Act (“California Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq., “CEQA”) and
  its implementing guidelines (14 California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.; “CEQA
  Guidelines”) for the following reasons: (1) it will not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable
  indirect physical change in the environment (CEQA Guidelines § 15060(c)(2)); (2) there is no
  possibility that the Ordinance itself may have a significant effect on the environment (CEQA
  Guidelines § 15061(b)(3)); and (3) the Ordinance, by itself, does not constitute a “project” as
  defined in the CEQA Guidelines (CEQA Guidelines § 15378). The Ordinance is for general
  policies and procedure-making; any project governed by the proposed Ordinance would receive
  a separate environmental evaluation and review. It can be seen with certainty that there is no
  possibility that the Ordinance may have a significant effect on the environment.

4-D.  A CONTINUED PUBLIC HEARING TO CONSIDER INTRODUCTION AND FIRST READING
  OF ZONING CODE AMENDMENT NO. 22-01 (ZCA-22-01), AN ORDINANCE ADDING THE
  MONTEREY PARK MUNICIPAL CODE, CHAPTER 21.19, ENTITLED “INCLUSIONARY
  HOUSING” TO IMPLEMENT THE MONTEREY PARK HOUSING ELEMENT.
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Opening a continued public hearing and taking testimonial and documentary evidence;
  (2)  After closing the public hearing and considering the evidence submitted during that public
  hearing to introduce and waive first reading of Ordinance No. _____ adding Chapter 21.19
  (Inclusionary Housing) to the Monterey Park Municipal Code to implement the Monterey
  Park Housing Element; and
  (3)  Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  Pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code § 21000, et seq.;
  “CEQA”) and its implementing regulations (14 Cal. Code of Regs. § 15000, et seq.; the "CEQA
  Guidelines”), the proposed Ordinance and Resolution (ZCA 22-01) are exempt from further
  CEQA review for the following reasons: (1) they will not result in a direct or reasonably
  foreseeable indirect physical change in the environment (CEQA Guidelines § 15060(c)(2)); (2)
  there is no possibility that the Ordinance may have a significant effect on the environment
  because any potential, future, housing projects would undergo separate environmental review
  (CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3)); and (3) the Ordinance and Resolution, by themselves, do not
  constitute a “project” as defined in the CEQA Guidelines because they involve a policy action
  that is legislative implementing affordable housing policy and affects prospective future housing
  development to comply with Housing Element Program 15 (CEQA Guidelines § 15378).

  b. Introducing and waiving first reading of an Ordinance approving a Development

  (3) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  The Project is consistent with the Supplemental Environmental Impact Report (“SEIR”) and
  Statement of Overriding Considerations certified (and adopted) by the City Council on
  December 19, 2012 via Resolution No. 11548 (State Clearinghouse No. 1999051058). None of

2.  OLD BUSINESS

2-A.  RECEIVE AND FILE STAFF REPORT SUMMARIZING THE STATUS OF
  EMERGENCY REPAIRS OF THE MONTEREY PASS ROAD WATER LINE

  On August 17, 2022, City Council adopted Resolution No. 2022-R69 authorizing
  the City Manager to take necessary measures for emergency repair of a water
  main line on Monterey Pass Road. Recurring water main leaks in several areas
  within Monterey Pass Road between the intersections of Vagabond Drive and
  Brightwood street resulted in extensive infrastructure damage to the roadway and
  necessary water main pipe repairs to ensure continued water service to residences
  and businesses in the area.

  On August 29, 2022, the City contracted with Cannon Corporation for professional
  engineering services to prepare design plans and specifications for the water
  pipeline replacement. Cannon provided the City with complete plans to replace the
  existing 12-inch water transmission line in December which was identified in the
  December 21, 2022 staff report update for this project.

  Following the adoption of the emergency resolution, staff contacted potential
  contractors and identified Ferreira Coastal Construction (Ferreira) in September
  2022 as a qualified contractor that also had the resources and availability for the
  construction phase of this project. Ferreira worked closely with the City and
  Cannon Corporation during the design phase to provide input on design,
  constructability, and material availability.

  Action Taken: The City Council received and filed the staff report summarizing
  the status of emergency repairs of the Monterey Pass Road water line.

  The Monterey Park Market Place development was originally approved through a

  MPMC Chapter 13.12 regulates encroachments and construction within all public
  right of ways within the City. The regulations under this chapter were first
  implemented in the 1980s and are stale in comparison to industry standards.
  The proposed ordinance updates regulations for excavations and encroachments
  on, over, and under public rights-of-ways and public service easements.

  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  This Ordinance was reviewed pursuant to CEQA. Adopting this Ordinance is
  exempt from further environmental review because it establishes rules and
  procedures for operation of existing facilities; minor temporary use of land; minor
  alterations in land use; new construction of small structures; and minor structures
  accessory to existing commercial facilities. The Ordinance, therefore, is
  categorically exempt from further environmental review under CEQA Guidelines
  §§ 15301; 15303, 15304(e); 15305; and 15311. Further, adopting the ordinance is
  exempt from environmental review pursuant to CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3)
  because the ordinance is for general policies and procedure-making. It can be
  seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the Ordinance may have a
  significant effect on the environment. Individual projects utilizing these regulations
  will each be separately subject to an environmental assessment. Finally, this
  Ordinance is exempt from further environmental review pursuant to CEQA
  Guidelines § 15269(a) because the protection of public and private property is
  necessary to maintain service essential to the public, health and welfare.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
It is requested that the City Council authorize the City Manager to engage a consulting
firm to assist the City in updating its 2010 Economic Development Strategic Plan.
Monterey Park’s economic landscape has rapidly evolved over the past decade and
accelerated even more with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore, updating
the City’s Strategic Plan is crucial to ensure the City’s continued economic growth,
competitiveness, and resilience. The Natelson Dale Group was identified as having the
knowledge, skills, and most favorable pricing structure to provide the City with an updated
Plan that aligns with the City Council’s current economic goals and positions Monterey
Park for long-term growth and success.

BACKGROUND:
The City of Monterey Park’s 2010 Economic Development Strategic Plan was last
updated 13 years ago. However, the City’s economic landscape rapidly evolved over the
past decade and intensified even more with the COVID-19 pandemic. Since then, the City
experienced significant changes in its economic landscape including industry trends,
technological advancements, and demographic patterns. To ensure sustained growth, job
creation, and an enhanced quality of life for residents, it is crucial that the Economic
Development Strategic Plan remains relevant and aligned with the changing needs of the
community. The benefit of engaging a qualified consultant to help update the City’s plan
includes the following:

Expertise and Specialized Knowledge: Working with a consultant specializing in
economic development strategic planning brings a wealth of expertise to Monterey Park.

studies, allowing us to make informed decisions that maximize current and future
economic potential.

Fresh Perspective: Engaging a consultant provides an external perspective for updating
Monterey Park’s economic development strategic plan. It brings objectivity to the process.

Rigorous Selection Process: To ensure transparency and fairness, the City staff
conducted a Request for Proposals (RFP) using a rigorous qualifications-based selection
process to identify the most suitable consulting firm for this project. The RFP solicited
proposals from multiple consulting firms with economic development strategic planning
expertise. The evaluation committee thoroughly reviewed and scored proposals based
on experience, qualifications, demonstrated success in similar projects at comparable
cities, approach to stakeholder engagement, and cost. As a result, the consulting firm
selected, The Dale Natelson Group, emerged as the top candidate due to its extensive
experience, proven track record, and competitive pricing.

Best Value for the City: The Natelson Dale Group was selected not only based on its

quality deliverables. The firm has extensive experience working with cities in the Los
Angeles and San Gabriel Valley area similar to Monterey Park, including a detailed 2019
market analysis for Monterey Park’s General Plan update.

analysis, stakeholder engagement activities, plan development and implementation, and

SUBJECT:  Tree Species Selections for Ongoing Sidewalk Improvements

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Approving the tree species listed in Exhibit A to be included in all applicable
  Public Works sidewalk hazard removal and replacement projects; and
  2. Taking such additional, related action that may be desirable.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

As part of the City exercising due diligence regarding continued sidewalk improvements
along residential sidewalks and business corridors in the public right of way, nuisance
trees causing infrastructure damage will be removed and replaced with less intrusive,
functionally suitable, and aesthetically pleasing trees. Staff completed an analysis of
tree species that will serve immediate needs and any subsequent required applications
of removal and replacement. Formal presentations were made to the Environmental
Commission and to Business District representatives within the past 60 days. These
presentations yielded positive input, interest and anticipation for the project to begin.

BACKGROUND:

On August 4, 2021, City Council was presented with a program overview containing
seven miles of City wide sidewalk survey data. This presentation identified and ranked
needed sidewalk improvements in high density foot traffic areas. The Public Works
Department identified the first phase of sidewalk project to be addressed. Many of these
locations have sidewalks that are in need of repair due to mature (40-50+years) Ficus,
Melaleuca, and Eucalyptus trees. Of the 63 locations in the first phase area of focus, 38
are caused by trees of these species.

Staff worked with West Coast Arborist (WCA) to complete a comprehensive tree master
plan which is anticipated to be completed before the end of this calendar year.
However, due to an upcoming project, some tree replacement options needed to be
identified now for replacement. As part of the tree master plan, staff and WCA
completed research and determined multiple species that are viable replacements for
this project. WCA has been the City’s contracted arborist for over 20 years and has a
comprehensive understanding of the region and the City’s climate, soil and community.
These chosen species have proven to meet the needs of modern and current urban
forestry applications. Considerations for chosen tree species include: parkway size,
planting area, soil conditions, powerline interference, growth rate, canopy shape and

  Page 34 of 410
 Staff Report
Page 2 of 2
June 7, 2023
size, sightline continuity, pest and wildlife factors, structural integrity, male vs. female,
California and Monterey Park zone hardiness rating (related to soil), existing site
density, shade rating, root intrusion rating, nursery availability, property value
enhancement, maintenance costs, commercial signage visibility, disease susceptibility,
flowering characteristics, deciduous vs. evergreen, sustainability, changes in ecosystem
dynamics, along with other factors. As part of this project and the finalization of the tree
master plan, staff will work with the community on changes and impacts to the urban
forestry.

To serve a community well, trees should be species having long life, with traits that
successfully demonstrate serving a 35 to 45 year planning horizon. The framework for
removal and planting should have a goal of “the right tree in the right place.” Emphasis
should also be made on species that can reduce the potential of recurring root damage
to sewer laterals, curbs, gutters and sidewalks. Tree selections should maximize the
natural benefits and functionality of the City’s urban forest, while also considering
contemporary factors such as carbon sequestration and climate adaption.

As part of the City’s community outreach efforts, staff met with the Environmental
Commission, held a workshop with businesses and published information regarding the
upcoming sidewalk project and related tree replacements in the Cascades newspaper.
Overall, the City has received positive feedback regarding the proposed tree species
that would be part of the upcoming sidewalk project and future community improvement
projects. Additionally, staff had informational material at its Public Works open house
event.

FISCAL IMPACT:

There is no fiscal impact with approving the list of proposed tree species.

 SUBJECT:  Resolution Identifying a Public Works Street Maintenance Project to be
  Included in the FY 2023-24 Budget and Funded by Senate Bill 1: The
  Road Repair and Accountability Act of 2017

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting a resolution identifying a street maintenance project to be included in the
  FY 2023-24 budget and funded with Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation Act
  (RMRA) funds, in a form approved by the City Attorney; and
  2. Take such additional, related action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
Senate Bill 1 (SB1), the Road Repair and Accountability Act of 2017 addresses the
significant multi-modal transportation funding shortfall statewide. As of November 2017,
portions of SB1 revenues are deposited into a Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation
Account (RMRA) and made available to eligible cities and counties, which must comply
with RMRA funding requirements as determined by the California Transportation
Commission (CTC).

RMRA funds made available for the Local Streets and Roads Funding Program are
prioritized for expenditure on basic road maintenance and rehabilitation projects, and on
critical safety projects. The CTC provided a number of example projects and uses for
RMRA funding that includes, but are not limited to, the following: Road Maintenance and
Rehabilitation, Safety Projects, Railroad Grade Separations, Complete Streets
Components (including active transportation purposes, pedestrian and bicycle safety
projects, transit facilities, and drainage and stormwater capture projects in conjunction with
any other allowable project), and Traffic Control Devices.

BACKGROUND:
The most recent State estimates for FY 2023-24 project Monterey Park will receive
$1,556,219 in RMRA funds. In order to be eligible to receive these funds, agencies must
submit a proposed project list to the CTC by July 1, 2023, along with budget support
documentation including the council meeting minutes and/or resolution of the City Council
committing to the project list. This year, project lists are due July 1, 2023.

The proposed capital improvement project includes the resurfacing of various local streets
as identified in the City’s Pavement Management Study, listed in the resolution. Staff

reviewed the study and selected those street segments that would most benefit from a
rehabilitation project based on their current conditions. Once the resolution is adopted and

primarily consists of grinding and overlay of the roadway surface with asphalt concrete and

SUBJECT:  Purchase of Parts and Materials for Pipelines

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Awarding three-year contracts to five vendors: Core & Main, LP, S & J Supply Co.,
  Inc., SoCal Compton Pipe Supply, United Water Works and Western Water Works
  Supply Co., in a form approved by the City Attorney, for a combined total not to
  exceed $500,000, annually, for the purchase of pipe supplies and related parts for
  the Water Division; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The Water Division purchases various pipe supplies and parts to maintain the City’s water
pipelines. Staff has solicited pricing from local vendors and requests that City Council
award contracts to all five companies: Core & Main, LP, S & J Supply Co., Inc., SoCal
Compton Pipe Supply, United Water Works and Western Water Works Supply Co. for the
purchase of parts and materials. The contracts will have a term of three-years and a
combined total not to exceed $500,000 annually.

BACKGROUND:
The Public Works Water Division expends between $300,000 to $500,000 annually on
water supplies such as pipes, valves and related parts for repair services and new or
upgrade installations. City employees install the parts and materials. In April 2023, staff
solicited pricing for commonly used parts that are categorized by the diameter of the pipe
part (e.g., 3/4" to 12"). Five suppliers responded to the bid: Core & Main LP, SoCal
Compton, S&J Supply Co., Inc., United Water Works, Inc. and Western Water Works
Supply Co.

A summary of their costs is provided in Attachment 1. Vendors set up contracts with
manufacturers to distribute their parts and sometimes vendors are not able to supply parts
for all manufacturers. United does not distribute Mueller parts so the highest cost for that
particular item - among the four other vendors - is entered into its cost proposal. This was
done in order to be able to compare total costs among the five companies.

could be detrimental to emergency projects such as watermain break repairs.

depending upon the lowest quote and/or delivery time. The request in this staff report to
award annual contracts will allow the City to purchase pipe supplies for a project as
needed.

Because the vendor’s circumstances with warehouse inventory, contractual relationships
with manufacturers and delivery options can impact its ability to provide certain parts in a
timely manner, contracts with all five vendors will ensure that parts are available when
needed. Staff is requesting the award of contracts to all five vendors: Core & Main, LP, S
& J Supply Co., Inc., SoCal Compton Pipe Supply, United Water Works and Western
Water Works Supply Co.

The FY2023 budget includes funds for parts and materials for pipelines. The funding
source for the purchase of these supplies is water operations funds (401) and water
treatment funds (402).

One of the streets listed in the table, New Avenue, is a shared street with the City of

The work for the entire project includes cold milling and removal of the existing asphalt

constructing new ADA curb ramps; replacing traffic loop detectors, restoring traffic striping
and pavement markings; and providing and maintaining traffic control during construction.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

In 1993 the City formed a citywide benefit assessment district to finance the operation and
maintenance of public street lighting and landscaping. The district was renewed each of
the past 30 years and must be renewed for 2023-24 in order for the City to continue
collecting assessments. The City started the process to renew its Citywide Maintenance
District No. 93-1 for the 2023-24 fiscal year at its April 5, 2023 meeting. At that time, the
City Council approved the Engineer's Report; adopted the Resolution of Intention
(Resolution No. 2023-R22) and scheduled the required public hearing for June 7, 2023.

The district renewal will follow the City Council’s action at the conclusion of the June 7th
public hearing.

BACKGROUND:

In 1993, the State implemented Education Revenue Augmentation (ERAF) transfer that
shifts property tax revenues from local governments to schools. The City’s loss from ERAF
was $1.2 million. In 1993, after considering various options to balance the budget, the City
formed a benefit assessment district pursuant to the 1972 Lighting and Landscaping Act
(Streets & Highways Code §§ 22500, et seq.). The assessment revenues are used to pay
for the costs for maintaining street lighting and public landscaping. The funds freed up by
the assessment revenues are used to maintain essential City services such as police, fire,
public works, recreation, and library.

The law requires the City to renew the assessments each year. Revenue generated by
the City’s assessment district is approximately $1,004,990 a year. The City has renewed
the benefit assessment district every year for the past 30 years. During this time, the rate
has only been increased once, in 1996 (from $39.97 to $40.97). Since 1996, the rates
have not been adjusted and the City continues using General-Fund monies to supplement
significant shortfalls that result from increased operating costs.

At its April 5, 2023 meeting, the City Council adopted a Resolution of Intention (Resolution
No. 2023-R22) which, among other things, proposes an assessment per single-family
home of $40.97 for 2023-24. The cost for the operation and maintenance of the City’s
landscaping and lighting is approximately $1.6 million. The benefit assessment district will
fund $1,004,990 of the cost and the City’s General Fund will cover the remaining $571,221.

The Resolution of Intention, which includes the public hearing date and protest procedures,
was published in the Monterey Park Press on May 16, 2023. To date, no majority protest
was received against the proposed assessment district renewal for 2023-24.

FISCAL IMPACT

The proposed assessment rates for 2023-24 are the same as they were for 2022-23. The
benefit assessment district will raise approximately $1,004,990 for 2023-24. If the
assessment district is not renewed, the City must reduce expenditures and/or seek new
revenues to balance the budget.

BOARD/COMMISSION REVIEW:

The Planning Commission, at its April 25, 2023 meeting reviewed this ordinance. With a
unanimous vote, the Commission recommended to Council to adopt the draft Ordinance
amending regulations related to Density Bonus under ZCA-23-01.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

On May 17, 2023, the City Council by a unanimous vote, continued the item to June 7,
2022.

In March of 2022, the City Council categorized an update of the Density Bonus Ordinance
as a moderate priority. On November 2, 2022, City Council asked Staff to bring forward
an update to the Density Bonus Ordinance in coordination with the Inclusionary Housing
Ordinance. On November 16, 2022, the City Council amended and adopted the 2021-
2029 Housing Element that included Program 14: Affordable Housing Development
Incentives, which identified an objective to consider updating the City’s Density
Ordinance.

BACKGROUND:

A density bonus is an incentive-based tool that permits a developer to increase the
maximum allowable development density on a site in exchange for specified public policy
goals. If adopted, the proposed Ordinance would provide density bonuses to help develop
affordable housing units in exchange for a menu of incentives to make development
easier. This is accomplished by reducing the applicable development standards such as
height, floor area ratio, and setbacks, among others.

Density bonus regulations are mandated by Government Code § 65915. The City’s
density bonus regulations were last updated in 2013 and there have been changes in
California law during the last ten years that require amendments to the MPMC. The
proposed Ordinance will reconcile the City’s regulations with applicable law.

ANALYSIS

If adopted, the Ordinance will implement Government Code §§ 65915, et seq.
(Attachment A). Currently, California law permits a bonus ranging from 20-80% density
increase, depending on how many affordable housing units the developer includes in a
project. Additionally, for projects that provide 100% affordable units, applicants are
allowed unlimited density bonus and an additional three stories of building height if
located near a major transit stop. Under the State law, the following are the minimum
thresholds that qualify a project for a density bonus:

    5% of units set-aside for very low income households;
    10% of units set-aside for lower income households ;
    10% of for-sale units set-aside for moderate income households ;

  Page 211 of 410
 Staff Report
Page 3 of 4
June 7, 2023

    100% of units set-aside for very low, low-, and moderate-income households (with
  maximum 20% moderate);
    10% of the housing units set-aside for transitional foster youth, disabled veterans
  or homeless persons, with rents restricted at the very low-income level;
    20% of units set-aside for low-income college students in housing dedicated for
  full-time students at accredited colleges;
    The project dedicates at least one acre of land, or land of sufficient size to permit
  at least 40 units, to the city for very low-income units and is appropriately zoned
  and includes access to public utilities and infrastructure;
    The project is a senior citizen housing development with at least 35 units (no
  affordable units required); and
    The project is a mobile home park this is age-restricted to senior citizens (no
  affordable units required)

As part of the update to the Density Bonus regulations, an updated menu of incentives is
included. This allows the City to prioritize relaxation of development standards. The menu
of incentives provides clarity to developers while preserving the City’s interests and
priorities. The menu of incentives includes:

    Reduction of yards and setbacks;
    Reduction of lot width requirements;
    Increase of floor area ratio;
    Increase in building height/total number of stories;
    Reduction of open space requirements;
    Expanded area for density calculation; and
    Sustainable “Green” Building compliance.

Newly added to the menu of incentives is an option for additional density bonus when a
development employs sustainable building practices, as prioritizing sustainable practices
is one of the City’s goals. This menu of incentives helps to preserve local control within
the City’s developable properties. Overall, the proposed Ordinance, if adopted, helps to
achieve goals and objectives set by City Council and the Housing Element, and is
consistent with California law.

  AN ORDINANCE AMENDING MONTEREY PARK MUNICIPAL CODE
  CHAPTER 21.18 GOVERNING AFFORDABLE HOUSING INCENTIVES
  AND DENSITY BONUS

  The City Council of the City of Monterey Park does ordain as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds and declares that:

  A. Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) Chapter 21.18 regulates density
  bonuses in the City and was last amended in 2013;

  B. The City initiated a code amendment by this Ordinance (“ZCA 23-01”) pursuant
  to MPMC § 21.38.020;

  C. In addition, the Director reviewed ZCA 23-01’s environmental impacts under
  the California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et
  seq., “CEQA”) and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 California Code
  of Regulations §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”);

  D. On April 25, 2023, the Planning Commission conducted a duly noticed public
  hearing to assess the proposed MPMC amendments in ZCA 23-01, considered
  all oral and written evidence, and adopted Planning Commission Resolution
  No. 03-23 recommending that the City Council adopt this Ordinance; and

  E. This Ordinance is adopted based upon the entirety of the administrative record
  including, without limitation, the staff reports submitted to the Planning
  Commission and City Council during the course of the public hearings.

SECTION 2: Zoning Amendments. Pursuant to MPMC § 21.38.050, the City Council
finds as follows:

  A. The MPMC amendments in this Ordinance are consistent with the goals,
  policies and objectives of the General Plan. Among other things, these
  regulations will provide housing opportunities for households in all income
  levels without constraining housing development in the City and implements
  Program 14 of the Housing Element.

  B. This Ordinance will not adversely affect surrounding properties. Regulations
  adopted by the Ordinance govern all property within the City’s jurisdiction and
  will not affect a change in the use or the intensity of use of property in any zone.

  C. This Ordinance promotes public health, safety, and general welfare and serves
  the goals and purposes of the MPMC’s zoning regulations. The density bonus
  regulations will continue to promote the public health, safety, and general

  Page 232 of 410

  welfare while serving the goals and purposes of the zoning regulations. Among
  other things, the regulations will facilitate creation of housing to address the
  Legislature’s determination regarding a statewide housing shortage for
  households of very low-, low-, and moderate-incomes, and bring the MPMC
  into compliance with State law.

SECTION 3: Environmental Review. The proposed Ordinance is exempt from additional
environmental review under the California Environmental Quality Act (“California Public
Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq., “CEQA”) and its implementing guidelines (14
California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.; “CEQA Guidelines”) for the following
reasons: (1) it will not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change
in the environment (CEQA Guidelines § 15060(c)(2)); (2) there is no possibility that the
Ordinance itself may have a significant effect on the environment (CEQA Guidelines §
15061(b)(3)); and (3) the Ordinance, by itself, does not constitute a “project” as defined
in the CEQA Guidelines (CEQA Guidelines § 15378). The Ordinance is for general
policies and procedure-making; any project governed by the proposed Ordinance would
receive a separate environmental evaluation and review. It can be seen with certainty that
there is no possibility that the Ordinance may have a significant effect on the environment.

SECTION 4: Chapter 21.18 of the Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) entitled
“AFFORDABLE HOUSING INCENTIVES—DENSITY BONUS” is amended in its entirety
to read as follows:

  “Chapter 21.18

  AFFORDABLE HOUSING INCENTIVES—DENSITY BONUS

21.18.010. Purpose and Intent
21.18.020. Procedures
21.18.030. Bonuses and Incentives
21.18.040. Amenities
21.18.050. Menu of Incentives

21.18.010.  Purpose.

  The purpose of this Chapter is to establish procedures for implementing
  density bonus requirements set forth in Government Code §§ 65915, et
  seq., as may be amended from time to time (the “Density Bonus Act”).

21.18.020.  Procedure.

  A.  In addition to any other requirement, applications for a density bonus must
  be filed on a form approved by the Community Development Director, or

  Page 233 of 410
 Ordinance No.
Page 3 of 7

  designee (the “Director”). An application must be filed concurrently with any
  other land use application required by this code. At the time the application
  is submitted, the applicant must pay an application fee established by City
  Council resolution.

  B.  The Director will process the Density Bonus Act application in the same
  manner as all applications required by this code.

  C.  Applications filed under this chapter must include reasonable
  documentation to establish eligibility under the Density Bonus Act.

21.18.030.  Bonuses and Incentives.

  A.  Housing developments qualifying under the Density Bonus Act may receive
  a bonus or concession pursuant to this chapter.

  B.  Terms and phrases used in this chapter have the same meaning as defined
  by the Density Bonus Act.

  C.  Where the density allowed under this code is inconsistent with the density
  allowed under the land use element of the general plan, the maximum
  density allowed controls.

  D.  Upon an applicant’s submission of reasonable documentation establishing
  eligibility, the City may not impose any development standard or parking
  standard that physically precludes a housing development qualifying under
  the Density Bonus Act.

  E.  Before the Building Official issues a building permit, an applicant receiving
  bonuses or concessions under this chapter must execute and record an
  agreement, in a form approved by the City Attorney, securing the continued
  affordability of all dwelling units in accordance with the Density Bonus Act
  and this chapter.

  F.  All dwelling units benefitting from the bonuses or concessions under this
  chapter must be concurrently built in the same manner as market rates. All
  affordable units must be integrated and reasonably distributed throughout
  the approved project with the market rate units to ensure a reasonable mix
  of affordable and market rate units.

21.18.040.  Amenities.

  Residents of affordable units may not be charged for amenities not charged to
  other residents including, without limitation, access to recreational facilities,
  parking, cable television, and interior amenities like dishwashers and microwave

  Page 234 of 410
 Ordinance No.
Page 4 of 7

  ovens. Optional services for all residents must be the same. Tenants of affordable
  units may not be required to purchase additional services.

21.18.050.  Menu of Incentives.

  Applicants with projects qualifying for incentives may request one or more of the
  following incentives the number of incentives being requested must be consistent
  to the Density Bonus Act unless otherwise authorized by the approving body:

  A.  Yard/Setback. Up to a 20% decrease in the required width or depth of any
  individual yard or setback, except along any property line that abuts a R-1
  or more restrictively zoned property. A landscaping plan must be submitted
  to the Director for approval that incorporates screening as defined by this
  title.

  B.  Lot Width. Up to a 20% decrease from a lot width requirement. A
  landscaping plan must be submitted to the Director for approval that
  incorporates screening as defined by this title.

  C.  Floor Area Ratio.

  1.  A percentage increase in the allowable floor area ratio equal to the
  percentage of density bonus for which the project is eligible, not to
  exceed 35%; or

  2.  In lieu of the otherwise applicable floor area ratio, a floor area ratio
  not to exceed those identified in the General Plan governing the
  project site.

  D.  Height. Subject to Chapter 21.42, a percentage increase in the height
  requirement in feet equal to the percentage of density bonus for which the
  project is eligible. This percentage increase in height is applicable over the
  entire parcel regardless of the number of underlying height limits. For
  purposes of this subsection, height limits contained in this Title and adopted
  specific plans do not apply.

  1.  In any zone in which the height or number of stories is limited, this
  height increase will permit a maximum of 11 additional feet or one
  additional story, whichever is lower, to provide the affordable units.

  2.  No additional height can be permitted for that portion of a building in
  a project that is located within 50 feet of a lot classified in an R-1 or
  more restrictive zone.

  3.  No additional height is permitted for that portion of a building in a
  project that is located within 15 feet of a lot classified in the R-2 Zone.

  Page 235 of 410
 Ordinance No.
Page 5 of 7

  4.  For each foot of additional height, the building must be set back one
  horizontal foot.

  5.  No additional height can be permitted for any portion of a building in
  a project located on a lot sharing a common lot line with or across an
  alley from a lot classified in an R-1 or more restrictive zone. This
  prohibition does not apply if the lot on which the project is located
  within 1,500 feet of a transit stop but no additional height can be
  permitted for that portion of a building in the project that is located
  within 50 feet of a lot classified in an R-1 or more restrictive
  residential zone.

  E.  Open Space. Up to a 20% decrease from an open space requirement. A
  landscaping plan must be submitted to the Director for approval that
  incorporates screening as defined by this title.

  F.  Density Calculation. The area of any land required to be dedicated for street
  or alley purposes may be included as lot area for purposes of calculating
  the maximum density permitted by the underlying zone in which the project
  is located.

  G.  Green Building. Density Bonus qualified projects that achieve compliance
  with Level 2 of the California Green Building Code may be provided with the
  following additional incentives that will not be counted toward the maximum
  incentives as permitted by California law:

  1.  Projects may be granted a density bonus of 20% additional units; or

  2.  Fifty percent of private open space may be credited toward
  satisfying common open space requirements if each dwelling unit,
  out of 50% of the total number of dwelling units, includes at least 50
  square feet of private open space with a minimum width and length
  of 5 linear feet. Alternatively, the project may comply with common
  open space requirements by providing private open space areas
  that exceed the minimum private open space requirements in this
  title, provided the private open space is equal to or greater than the
  total common open space area required for the development in this
  title.

21.18.060.  Request for Incentives.

  A.  For projects qualifying under the Density Bonus Act for which ministerial
  approvals are required, the following procedures apply:

  1.  Application. An applicant must file a request on a form provided by
  the Director, accompanied fees established by city council
  resolution.

  2.  Director Authority. The Director may determine whether an
  application is consistent with this chapter.

  B.  Action. The Director must approve a density bonus and requested
  incentive(s) unless the Director makes one or more of the written findings
  provided for under Government Code § 65915(d)(1).

  C.  Written Decision. The Director must transmit a written decision by first class
  mail to the applicant and to all owners of properties abutting, and across the
  street or alley from the subject property.

21.18.070. Additional Option for Affordable Units Located Near Transit Stop/
Major Employment Center.

  In lieu of providing the requisite number of affordable units in a project located in
  or within 1,500 feet of a transit stop or major employment center, as determined
  by the Director, that would otherwise be required under this Chapter an applicant
  may opt to provide a greater number of smaller units provided that:

  A.  The total number of units in the project, including density bonus units, do
  not exceed the maximum permitted by this chapter;

  B.  The square footage of the aggregate smaller affordable units is equal to or
  greater than the square footage of the aggregate affordable units that would
  otherwise be required under this chapter;

  C.  The smaller affordable units are distributed throughout the building and
  have proportionally the same number of bedrooms as the market rate units;
  and

  D.  The smaller affordable units meet the minimum unit size requirements
  established by the Low Income Housing Tax Credit Program (4 Cal. Code
  of Regs. § 10300, et seq.).”

Program 15 of the Monterey Park Housing Element provides that the City Council will

land dedication option be included in the ordinance, and referred the matter back to the

The Ordinance (Attachment 1) would encourage the production of affordable units in new
housing developments. This is accomplished by several methods, or a combination of
methods: (1) require actual construction of affordable units; (2) payment of an in-lieu fee
to the City that commensurate with the cost of a the “affordability gap” between the market
and affordable rate for the new unit or the construction of off-site affordable units within
the City; (3) construction of affordable units at an off-site location within the City, and/or
(4) dedication of land for the purpose of constructing affordable units within the City.

BACKGROUND:

The City adopted the 2021-2029 Housing Element of the General Plan on January 19,
2022; it was certified on March 20, 2023. Housing Element Program 15 provides that the
City Council will consider an inclusionary housing program. Such programs require
certain residential and mixed-use developments to designate a percentage of units within
the development as affordable housing. Alternatively, a developer may construct off-site
units or pay a fee or dedicate land in the City for the creation of affordable units.

On September 7, 2022, the City Council discussed potential inclusionary housing
standards. The Council generally supported inclusionary housing requirements and
directed the City Manager to develop an ordinance.

that the City Council adopt the draft Ordinance, which was considered by City Council on

Affordable Housing Trust Fund monies would be utilized, allowing developers an option
to dedicate land for the development of affordable units, and provide more information on
density bonuses. Council directed the Director to make further changes to the
Inclusionary Housing Ordinance and refer the matter back to the Planning Commission
for review and recommendation.

21.19.060 Standards for Inclusionary Housing Units.

A. Projects with inclusionary housing units are subject to the following requirements:

  facilities available to market rate units at the same or lower cost chargeable, if at

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The Monterey Park Market Place development was originally approved through a Precise
Plan (PP-12-01) that was intended to redevelop a brownfield site to help stimulate the
local economy and create jobs while preserving the environment and public safety of the
area. Since the creation and implementation of PP-12-01, Phase 1 is complete, but
Phases 2 and 3 remains unbuilt. Phase 2 includes the wrap-around road south of the
Leachate Treatment Plant (LTP) and Thermal Destruction Facility (TDF), and Phase 3 is
the built-out of the area west of the LTP/TDF.

In recent years, market forces changed the way in which consumers conduct business: a
decreased need for traditional brick-and-mortar stores and an increased demand for last
mile facilities, warehouses, auto dealerships, and sound stages for the entertainment
industry emerged since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. The applicant seeks
to create flexibility to allow for land uses that help address the changing landscape of the
commercial/service sector by providing a framework through the proposed Market Place
Specific Plan (“MPSP”) to allow for such uses. No immediate construction or development
is proposed at this time.

The Project includes the proposed adoption of the MPSP to address the eventual build-
out of the Market Place; it supersedes the existing Precise Plan. The Specific Plan will be
identified within the Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) and the entire Market Place
Project site will be re-zoned from the Regional Specialty Center with Planned
Development Overlay, to the MPSP. Further, the amended and restated Development
agreement between the City and the Applicant will help ensure that the eventual build-
out of the Market Place will provide a public benefit to the community.

Most recently, the City Council considered a similar proposal of the site that was not
approved at its April 19, 2023 meeting. Following that date, on May 15, 2023, the
applicant submitted a new application. That application includes a revised Specific Plan
that includes new uses that would be permitted at the site for additional Council
consideration.

BACKGROUND:

The City Council approved the Market Place development on December 19, 2012 by
adopting PP-12-01 to regulate its development. The Market Place property is comprised
of 63.68 acres, with a General Plan land use designation of Commercial and zoning of
Regional Specialty Center (R-S), with a Planned Development (P-D) overlay. Ten parcels
make up the site that includes all current commercial development anchored by Costco
and Home Depot, with several other retail and service businesses, and multiple
commercial eating establishments or restaurants, some of which include drive-throughs.

The developed areas are accessed from Market Place Drive which is off Potrero Grande
Drive in the city and Paramount Boulevard in Montebello. There are also existing
Leachate Treatment Plant (LTP) and Thermal Destruction Facility (TDF) facilities (which
are not part of the Monterey Park Market Place commercial development), but contained
within the subject site and the MPSP. The western portion of the site, west of the LTP/TDF
operations, remains vacant (Phase 3). The subject site is surrounded by Southern
California Edison facilities to the north, west, and east, and the 60 Freeway to the south
(see Figure 1).

Zoning Code Amendment

The applicant requests that the City Council approve Zoning Code Amendment (ZCA-23-
03) to adopt the MPSP (SP-23-01). This will establish a Specific Plan Zone in the
Municipal Code and include the regulatory document of the Specific Plan, that will govern
development within the subject site. The MPSP represents a tool for development to
systematically implement the General Plan and the individual development proposals in
the Market Place Phase 3 project area.

Contained within the MPSP are development standards permitted within the subject site,
including the additional development of Phase 3 to allow for uses which were not
previously permitted or contemplated as part of PP-12-01. As identified in the Specific
Plan, the uses listed below for Phase 3 of the project may include:

  •  Construction of a last mile distribution center of up to 97,000 square feet of floor
  area;
  •  Construction of a warehouse of up to 175,000 square feet of floor area;
  •  Construction of an automobile dealership with a collision or service center totaling
  up to 100,000 square feet of floor area; or
  •  Construction of up to 150,000 square feet of floor area of retail uses.

When the PP 12-01 was approved, the anticipated build-out of Phase 3 included retail
uses, which remains on the list of development options. However, as the commercial and
retail market has changed in the last 10 years, the developer’s ability to build out with
retail uses has become less easily achieved. The additional uses of a last-mile distribution
center, a warehouse, or an automobile dealership are proposed alternate uses. The
proposed Specific Plan sets up the framework to allow the above listed uses.

With the additional alternative uses proposed in the Market Place Specific Plan, the
applicant has included a Level of Service and Vehicle Miles Traveled Screening Analysis
to support an auto dealership which will result in fewer trips generated than the build-out
of Phase 3 with retail uses analyzed as part of the FEIR and SEIR for the overall project.
In a case where, a last mile distribution center or warehouse use is proposed, a similar
traffic analysis will be necessary to ensure that those developments are not exceeding
the traffic that was contemplated in the SEIR.

The proposed Specific Plan is consistent with the applicable General Plan Elements of
the Land Use, Circulation, Safety and Community Service, Resource, and housing Goals
and Policies as analyzed in the General Plan. Overall, the Specific Plan contains unique
development standards and design guidelines to ensure that commercial development
will be compatible with the site and existing development around the Specific Plan Area.
This is accomplished through the inclusion of design guidelines addressing the
architectural design for the future development at the Market Place.

Zone Change

With the creation of the MPSP Zone and its Specific Plan as described above, it is
proposed that the entire site that includes 10 parcels and is 63.68 acres in size be
rezoned from its current zoning of Regional Specialty Center (R-S), with a Planned
Development (P-D) overlay, to the MPSP Zone (ZA-23-01). This new MPSP Zone is
consistent with the General Plan Land Use Designation of Commercial, since the
underlying uses permitted within the MPSP are a broad range of retail and service
commercial uses. All uses that are currently existing at the site or have been previously
approved will remain as permitted uses, with the additional uses listed in the Specific
Plan being permitted as well.

Development Agreement

Chapter 21.44 of the MPMC requires Development Agreements (DA) for large scale
projects that require multiple entitlements and long-term commitment of both public and
private resources. The original approval of the Market Place included a DA that was
approved in 2013. However, with the new scenarios presented in Phase 3 of the project,
a new DA (DA-23-01) is proposed to allow for the uses proposed and an updated public
benefit payment. While the MPMC generally imposes a term of five years for development
agreements – which is intended to facilitate the prompt development of approved projects
– the City Council may change the term in its discretion. Here, the draft DA proposes an
initial term of five years with two automatic renewals of two years each; these renewals
would occur unless the DA were terminated not later than 90 days before the anniversary
date (Section 20 of the DA). As a result, the applicant would have an extended time within
which to construct improvements and the City would receive additional public benefit
payments as contemplated by Section 6(c) of the DA. Assuming that the DA were in effect
for the full nine-year term and the development was fully built out, the City could receive
up to approximately $1.6M in public benefit payments.

Previous Application

As the Council is aware, it previously considered this matter in April 2023. On April 19,
2023, the City Council voted 2-1-1 (Mayor pro tem Wong declared a conflict and was not
counted as part of the quorum) to adopt the draft ordinances that would have approved a
previous version of this project. California law requires an affirmative three votes to adopt
an ordinance. Consequently, the ordinances were not adopted.

Ordinarily, when an application for a discretionary permit is denied, a new application
cannot be filed for one year from the date of denial (MPMC § 21.32.140). Both this
application – and its previous version – seek only legislative actions by the City Council.
Consequently, the one year moratorium on a substantially similar project for the same
site does not apply.

   I. INTRODUCTION

  This Monterey Park Market Place Specific Plan (Specific Plan) was prepared in conformity with
  Government Code § 65451, et seq. Together with zoning regulations adopted by the Monterey
  Park Municipal Code (MPMC) and other Applicable Law (defined below), this Specific Plan sets
  forth the regulations for the development and operation of the Monterey Park Market Place
  project (Project or the Market Place).

  Pursuant to Government Code § 65450, a specific plan must include text and a diagram or
  diagrams, which specify all of the following in detail:

  •  The distribution, location, and extent of the uses of land, including open space within the
  area covered by the plan.
  •  The proposed distribution, location, extent, and intensity of major components of public
  and private transportation, sewage, water, drainage, solid waste disposal, energy and
  other essential facilities proposed to be located within the land area covered by the plan
  and needed to support the land uses described in the plan.
  •  Standards and criteria by which development will proceed, and standards for the
  conservation, development, and utilization of natural resources, where applicable.
  •  A program of implementation measures, including regulations, programs, public works
  projects and financing measures necessary to carry out the above items.
  •  A discussion of the relationship of the Specific Plan to the General Plan.

  This Specific Plan is compatible and consistent with the goals and policies outlined in the City of
  Monterey Park’s General Plan (General Plan). This Specific Plan will further the goals and policies
  of the General Plan as more fully described below.

  This Specific Plan was prepared to provide the essential relationship between the policies of the
  General Plan and actual development in the Project area. By functioning as a regulatory
  document, the Specific Plan provides a means of implementing the General Plan. All future
  development within the Specific Plan boundaries must be consistent with the standards set forth
  in this document.

A.  SPECIFIC PLAN AREA
  This Specific Plan regulates real property (a triangular-shaped parcel consisting of approximately
  63.68 acres) located in the southeast portion of the City of Monterey Park, in the County of Los
  Angeles, State of California, immediately north of the Pomona Freeway, State Route 60 (Pomona
  Freeway), and west of Paramount Boulevard as shown on Figure 1 (Specific Plan Area).

  On or about December 19, 2012, the Monterey Park City Council adopted (a) Resolution No.
  11549 approving the Monterey Park Market Place Precise Plan (PP-12-01) and Tentative Tract
  Map No. 071549 (TM-12-01) and certifying the Supplemental Environmental Impact Report (SCH
  NO. 1999051058); and (b) Resolution No. 11548 a statement of overriding considerations for the
  Monterey Park Market Place Precise Plan. On or about January 16, 2013, the City Council adopted
  Ordinance No. 2094, approving a Development Agreement between the City of Monterey Park
  and Monterey Park Retail Partners, LLC to allow the development of the Monterey Park Market
  Place. The Monterey Park Market Place Precise Plan covered the same geographical location as
  the Specific Plan Area.

  Although part of the USEPA-designated OII landfill superfund site, the Monterey Park Market
  Place does not contain any hazardous materials and consists of two distinct areas. The Market
  Place portion that is to the east and north of Market Place Drive (which Drive is currently
  designated as APN 5275-003-026 and -027) is comprised of various tax parcels that have been
  largely developed with approximately 310,000 square feet of retail floor area:

  2. APN 5275-003-038:  A retail home improvement center.

  3. APN 5275-003-029, -037 and -039:  Various retail uses.

  The Market Place portion that is to the west of Market Place Drive and north of Pomona Highway
  (SR 60) is currently designated as APN 5275-003-025 and was not redeveloped. Between the two
  areas of the Market Place development, APN 5275-003-024 is the existing Leachate Treatment
  Plant (LTP) and Thermal Destruction Facility (TDF) facilities (which are not part of the Monterey
  Park Market Place development) but contained within the Specific Plan

  The Monterey Park Market Place area also includes various easements on the adjacent SCE parcel
  for grading, utilities, parking, drainage, and other permitted uses (collectively, the SCE

  Director or Planning Commission to approve modifications allowing up to 600,000 square feet.

   II. SPECIFIC PLAN OVERVIEW

A.  PURPOSE AND AUTHORITY OF THE SPECIFIC PLAN
  This Specific Plan is intended to provide for the orderly and efficient development of the Specific
  Plan Area in accordance with the provisions of the General Plan. In conjunction with the General
  Plan, the Specific Plan implements the plan for the physical development of the Specific Plan Area
  and a guide to all future development within the plan area.

  A Specific Plan may be prepared for any defined geographic area, which might benefit from
  specialized land use regulations and development standards.

  The Specific Plan provides for development within the Specific Plan Area and establishes the
  permitted uses, development intensity, site planning and development standards, design and
  architecture, landscaping, signs, refuse facilities, access and circulation, parking, and trip
  reduction measures of the Project.

B.  SPECIFIC PLAN SCOPE AND GOALS
  Implementation of General Plan goals and policies will occur through the establishment of land
  use designations, traffic circulation patterns, development policies, and the identification of
  backbone infrastructure necessary to support the planned intensity of development.

  To achieve this purpose, the Specific Plan has the following goals:

  1. Establish the planning concept, design theme, development regulations, and procedures
  necessary to achieve an orderly and compatible development;
  2. Implement the goals, policies, and objectives of the General Plan;
  3. Establish a framework to create a successful Project with a mix of predominantly retail
  uses with retail-supporting uses, such as Last Mile Distribution Center and Warehouse
  uses;
  4. Meet changing market demands for more home delivery by allowing car sales, Last Mile
  Distribution Center and Warehouse uses;
  5. Facilitate the full build-out of the Specific Plan Area; and
  6. Provide clear design guidelines and standards to allow for flexibility in the implementation
  and build-out of planned development within the Specific Plan area.

A.  DEVELOPMENT CONCEPT
  The Specific Plan provides a framework for developing approximately 63.68-acres in the

  Project while remaining consistent with Monterey Park’s suburban character.

  New development of Individual Projects may be based on one of the Conceptual Development
  Plans (see Figures 4A, 4B, 4C, and 4D). Development options other than the Conceptual
  Development Plans are permissible as set forth in the Specific Plan.

C.  GRADING CONCEPT
  Grading plans for an Individual Project’s building pads, roadways, pedestrian paths, water, sewer,
  and other utilities will be developed as needed for each Individual Project. Grading may consist
  of over excavation of soils beneath proposed buildings, to a depth of three to four feet, to remove
  unsuitable building material.

  Limited import for Individual Projects may be necessary, and is permissible, to stabilize soils
  depending upon the final geotechnical recommendations of a soils engineer.

  All grading must be accomplished pursuant to a Grading Plan that contains the following:

  a. Best management practices (BMPs).
  b. Non-paved areas must be revegetated or restored promptly after installation of utilities
  using drought-resistant, fast-growing vegetation that would quickly stabilize exposed
  ground surfaces. Alternative materials rather than reseeding (e.g., gravel) may be used in
  accordance with the Director’s direction.
  c. Runoff must be conveyed in accordance with the approved site drainage plans.
  d. Energy dissipaters or similar devices may be required at the end of drainpipe outlets to
  minimize erosion during storm events.
  e. Grading cannot occur during the wet season (November 1-April 15) unless erosion control
  devices acceptable to the City are implemented.

  slabs is provided and so that water does not pond near proposed structures or

  IV. EXISTING UTILITIES AND INFRASTRUCTURE

  The intent of this Section is to ensure that the Specific Plan Area is developed to support
  development of the proposed land uses and that on-site and off-site infrastructure systems have
  adequate capacity to serve the Project at build-out.

  Development of Individual Projects may require improving existing infrastructure and services in
  the Specific Plan Area. Basic utilities, including, water, sewer, and other utilities already exist on-
  site.

  The Government Code requires that a specific plan include text and diagrams that specify “the
  proposed distribution, location, and extent and intensity of major components of public and
  private transportation, sewage, water, drainage, solid waste disposal, energy, and other essential
  facilities proposed to be located within the area covered by the plan and needed to support the
  land uses described in the plan.”

  This Section of the Specific Plan fulfills this requirement and meets the MPMC requirements for
  the preparation of specific plans. In addition, this Section facilitates orderly development by
  identifying “backbone” utility infrastructure needed to support the proposed development.

E.  SITE PLANNING STANDARDS
  Site Planning Standards are those provisions that affect the site planning of an Individual
  Project. The categories that relate to this Specific Plan are building height, setback, and
  parking.

  1. Building Height – Building height within the Specific Plan Area is limited to 80 feet, as
  measured from the adjacent grade. Architectural features are allowed to project an
  additional 15 feet above the roof line.
  2. Floor Area Ratio – Floor Area Ratio (FAR) is limited to 0.65.
  3. Setback – The Site is surrounded by SCE’s right-of-way and the Pomona Freeway. The Site
  must maintain a 30-foot setback from property lines adjacent to a public Right-of-Way
  and the Freeway. The Specific Plan Area is allowed to have zero-foot setback from
  property lines adjacent to the SCE Easement Areas. All setbacks must be clear to the sky
  but may include roadways, utility infrastructure, loading, parking, landscaping, and fences
  and walls.
  4. Aisle Width – Parking areas must use a minimum of 24-foot aisle widths for two-way
  configurations and a minimum of 12-foot widths for one-way configurations. Parking area
  aisle widths must be a minimum provide for a minimum 25-foot back-out area for parking
  spaces. Standard parking stalls must be a minimum 9’ x 18’ stall size. Compact parking
  spaces are permitted pursuant to Section V.E.5 below.
  5. Parking Standards – The Site must comply with Applicable Law for handicapped parking
  area. All such parking stalls must be located reasonably near the storefronts for easy
  access and be striped and signed in a manner clearly showing the layouts of each parking
  space.
  6. Compact Spaces – The Site may include compact parking spaces. Compact spaces are
  those reduced from the standard 9’ x 18’ to 7 ‘ 6 “ x 16’. Compact stalls may not total
  more than 22% of the total required parking space on the site and must be clearly marked
  as “COMPACT,” with a site layout design approved by the Director.
  7. Loading Standards – Every warehousing/storage/light industrial tenant space must be
  provided with at least one off-street loading dock, bay, or space for every 25,000 square
  feet of gross floor area. The loading space must be a minimum of 12’ width x 40’ length x
  14’ height. Loading docks or bays must be provided for users that require truck loading
  spaces and that contain more than 50,000 square feet of floor area. Truck loading bays or
  docks must be located to allow for trucks to back into bays. All loading bays must be
  screened from sight from the public right-of-way.

d. Boundaries – The use of 400-watt 1-way entablature with 30-foot shoebox poles shall
  be situated and maintained along the boundaries of the Site or a 2-way entablature
  along the main drive aisle that connects Market Place Drive and Greenwood Avenue
  to serve both the main drive aisle and the adjacent parking. The illumination will not
  only identify the Project perimeter but also support security measures within the
  retail center and the parking areas that are located along the boundary of the Site.
e. Freeway Boundary – Proper lighting will be placed and maintained along the Pomona
  Freeway edge of the Site to enhance the development.
f. Illumination Intensity – Light spill beyond parking lots or roadways on the perimeter
  of the Site may not be greater than 0.5 footcandles. Light sources must be shielded
  and focused to reduce visibility from residential areas and the adjacent Pomona
  Freeway, while maintaining public safety and adequate lighting to ensure sign
  visibility.
g. Security – All buildings and structures must provide proper lighting fixtures to
  illuminate the areas at the back of each store and the side of each building to assure
  proper visibility and security. Except as otherwise expressly provided in the Specific
  Plan, the minimum lighting level for the Specific Plan Area is one footcandle.
h. Indirect lighting – Indirect illumination of building and landscaping will be utilized to
  accentuate architectural features, to create interest on large wall sections, and to
  uplight trees and water features. The lighting plan requires Director approval.
i.  Illumination Levels – Use of a variety of lighting height levels at entries, plazas, parking
  lots, landscaping, fountains, and other areas where evening activity is expected to
  create an exciting nighttime environment.
j.  Decorative Lighting – Decorative light poles with ornamentation associated with the
  design style will be installed and maintained in pedestrian areas and walkways.
  Decorative wall lights must also be incorporated into storefront designs at regular
  intervals.
k. Entryway – Decorative light poles will be located along Market Place Drive to accent
  the roadways leading into the main interior retail area and provide a smooth
  transition of decorative lighting to standard interior lighting fixtures. Along with other
  amenities, these lighting designs and locations are formulated to promote pedestrian
  friendliness, as well as safety and security.

I.  REFUSE FACILITIES
  For proper waste management practices, trash enclosures and/or equipment will be strategically
  located in the rear of each building, if feasible. Gates must be six-foot-high. Major tenants may
  have their own waste management areas within their building footprints to maintain the proper
  visual aesthetics of the Specific Plan Area. Public waste management will be accomplished by
  placing on-site furniture, such as waste receptacles and ash urns, throughout the Site. To
  minimize solid waste generated by the Project, the following measures must be implemented:

  1. Construction Phase – During Project construction, the following practices must be
  implemented to the maximum extent feasible:
  a. Off-site locations for construction waste exported from the Site and options for
  disposal of excess material should be identified. These options may include recycling
  of materials on-Site, sale to a broker or contractor, sale to a project in the vicinity, or
  transport to an environmentally cleared landfill.

  28

  Page 311 of 410
   b. Individual Project applicants should offer recyclable building materials, such as
  asphalt or concrete for sale or removal by private firms or public agencies for use in
  construction of other projects, if all cannot be reused on the Site.
  2. Operation Phase – During Project operations, the following practices must be
  implemented, to the maximum extent feasible, by the Project tenants within their
  buildings and will be specified in lease agreements between the Applicant and individual
  tenants:
  a. Recovery of materials such as aluminum and cardboard;
  b. Collection of office paper for recycling;
  c. Collection of polystyrene (foam) cups for recycling;
  d. Collection of glass, plastics, kitchen grease, laser printer toner cartridges, oil,
  batteries, and scrap metal for recycling or recovery.
  3. Design Features – The Applicant(s), tenants, and/or owner(s) of the Specific Plan Area are
  required to implement design features to support solid waste reduction programs, such
  as:
  a. Identifying the location and design of on-site recycling facilities;
  b. Providing on-site recycling receptacles to encourage recycling;
  c. Facilitating cardboard recycling (especially in retail areas) by providing adequate
  space and centralized locations for collection and bailing;
  d. Providing trash compactors for non-recycling materials to reduce the total volume of
  solid waste and the number of trips required for collection; and
  e. Providing on-site recycling receptacles in feasible locations accessible to the public to
  encourage recycling for all businesses, employees, and patrons.

K.  TRIP REDUCTION AND TRAVEL DEMAND MEASURES
  Reduction of trip and travel demand measures are provided in accordance with Applicable Law.
  Before any development is approved within the Specific Plan Area, Applicant(s) must provide for
  all of the following applicable transportation demand management and trip reduction measures
  to promote better air quality. The Project must comply with the Development Standards for

  29

  Page 312 of 410
 Nonresidential Development of 100,000 square feet and also provide all of the following
measures to the satisfaction of the Director and Public Works Director:

  1. Displayed Information – A bulletin board, display case, or kiosk displaying transportation
  information located where the greatest number of employees are likely to see it.
  Information must include, without limitation, the following:
  a. Current maps, routes and schedules for public transit serving the Site;
  b. Telephone numbers for referrals on transportation information, including numbers
  for regional ridesharing agency and local transit operators;
  c. Ridesharing promotional materials supplied by commuter-oriented organizations;
  d. Bicycle route and facility information, including regional/local bicycle maps and
  bicycle information;
  e. A list of facilities available for car-poolers, vanpoolers, bicyclists, transit riders and
  pedestrians at the Site.
  2. Van Pool – Not less than 10% of employee parking area must be located as close as is
  practical to the employee entrance(s), and be reserved for use by potential
  carpool/vanpool vehicles, without displacing handicapped and customer parking needs.
  A statement that preferential carpool/vanpool spaces for employees are available and a
  description of the method for obtaining such spaces must be included on the required
  transportation information board. Spaces will be signed/striped as demand warrants.
  Adequate turning radii and parking space dimensions shall also be included in van pool
  parking areas.
  3. Bicycles – Bicycle racks or other secure bicycle parking must be provided:
  a. To accommodate four bicycles per the first fifty thousand square feet of
  nonresidential developments;
  b. One bicycle per each additional fifty thousand square feet of nonresidential
  development. Calculations, which result in a fraction of 0.5 or higher, shall be rounded
  up to the nearest whole number;
  c. Bicycle facilities, such as showers, lockers, and changing spaces, must be provided for
  every tenant employing more than 80 employees per shift, and separate facilities for
  all genders must be provided for tenants employing more than 160 employees per
  shift;
  d. A bicycle parking facility may also be fully enclosed space or locker accessible only to
  the owner or operator of the bicycle, which protects the bike from inclement weather,
  e.g., racks, lockers, or locked room, must be provided.

 4. Safety – A safe and convenient zone in which vanpool and carpool vehicles may deliver or
  board their passengers.
5. Sidewalks – Sidewalks or other designated pathways following direct and safe routes must
  be maintained from the external pedestrian circulation system to each building in the
  development.
6. Circulation – Safe and convenient access must be maintained from the external circulation
  system to bicycle parking facilities on Site.
7. Employee Parking – Employee parking must be adequately provided within the total
  number of parking spaces planned for the Site. During peak shopping periods, off-site
  parking for employees may be instituted.
8. Roadway and Intersection Improvements –
  Applicant(s) are responsible for on-site roadways and intersections improvements and
  off-site improvements (collectively, the Traffic Improvements) as required by the
  Director.

  The Applicant(s) must seek approval for timely construction of the Traffic Improvements
  from all affected public entities, including the City of Montebello and CalTrans. Before the
  City issues a building permit for any Individual Project, the Applicant must establish
  assurances, to the satisfaction of the City Engineer and/or other approving agencies, for
  the construction of the Traffic Improvements. Before the City issues a final certificate of
  occupancy, the Applicant must provide improvement design plans satisfactory to the City
  Engineer and/or other approving agencies and construct all the Traffic Improvements. For
  any Traffic Improvements under the jurisdiction of the City of Montebello and/or CalTrans
  that have not been completed before the Applicant seeks its first certificate of occupancy
  for an Individual Project, the City may issue a temporary certificate of occupancy,
  provided that the Applicant first provides to the City written documentation confirming
  that another party committed sufficient funds for the construction of the Traffic
  Improvements required to be constructed at that time. Should the Applicant fail to
  provide such confirmation, the Applicant must place adequate funds (as mutually agreed
  upon by the Project applicant and the applicable entity) to fully construct such
  improvements in an escrow account to be used only for construction of the off-site
  improvements. Should the applicable entity does not approve plans to construct the off-
  site improvements within five years from the date the Applicant deposits such funds, any
  funds not being used to complete planned improvements will be returned to the
  Applicant.

  1. Supersedes MPMC Requirements. Where this Specific Plan contains language or
  standards that require more parking or permit less parking than the MPMC, this Specific
  Plan supersedes the MPMC.
  2. Parking Requirements. Individual Projects must provide parking in accordance with
  MPMC requirements for each proposed use, taking into account opportunities for shared
  parking with other proposed and existing uses and existing parking spaces.
  3. Alternative-Fueled Vehicles. Preferential parking spaces for alternative-fueled vehicles,
  including electric vehicles and/or compressed natural gas, must be provided in the Site as
