  recharging stations with both conductive and inductive charging capabilities. In no event,
  however, may the Site provide fewer vehicle charging stations than required by
  Applicable Law.

M.  TRIP GENERATION
  The Director must confirm that the number of a.m., p.m., and Saturday peak hour and daily trips
  for a proposed Individual Project, based on a trip generation memorandum prepared by the
  Applicant’s transportation engineer, to determine whether or not such trips would cause the Trip
  Cap to be cumulatively exceeded. The Applicant may receive a trip credit for an existing or
  previous entitlement and/or use that was or will be discontinued.

  Trips for an Individual Project having more than one use will be calculated by adding together the
  trips generated by the portion of floor area of the Project devoted to each use unless the Director,
  based on reasonable methods, determines otherwise.

  The Applicant’s trip generation memorandum will be based on the then-current Institute of
  Transportation Engineers (ITE) Trip Generation Handbook, or such alternative rates determined
  to be appropriate by the Applicant’s transportation engineer and approved by the Director. The
  determination of trips will reflect diverted and pass-by traffic trips, the effect of interaction of
  on-site mixed-use development, the proximity of the Project to mass transit facilities, and
  implementation of other transportation demand management measures.

  If the Director disagrees with any of the trip generation factors as applied to an Individual Project,
  the Applicant may submit a proposed alternative trip generation factor for the Project, along with
  a traffic generation study prepared by transportation engineer, for review by the Planning
  Agency. Upon receiving such a study from the Applicant, the Director will cause the City Clerk to
  schedule a public hearing before the Monterey Park Planning Agency in accordance with the
  MPMC. Within 45 days after conducting a public hearing, the Planning Agency will issue written

   findings that approve, disapprove, or conditionally approve the proposed alternative Trip
  generation factor as the Trip generation factor for the Individual Project.

  VI. INDIVIDUAL PROJECT APPROVALS

A.  PROJECT CLEARANCES AND ADMINISTRATIVE DESIGN REVIEW
  1. Unless otherwise exempt, an Applicant must obtain a Project Clearance from the Director
  before the City issues any permit for an Individual Project.
  2. The Director will issue a Project Clearance if the Individual Project is in substantial
  conformance with applicable provisions of this Specific Plan and other Applicable Law and
  the applicable mitigation measures from the SEIR in Appendix A.
  3. The Applicant must pay the necessary fees consistent with the provisions of this Specific
  Plan and other Applicable Law.
  4. The Director will approve, without change or modification, an Individual Project if it is
  substantially consistent with a Conceptual Development Plan and the design
  requirements of this Specific Plan. An Applicant may submit an alternative site plan, which
  the Director will review as provided in Section A.2 above.
  5. The Director’s approval of an Individual Project also constitutes an administrative
  clearance of design review pursuant to MPMC § 21.36.060.
  6. Should the Director determine that an Individual Project is inconsistent with the
  Conceptual Development Plans or other requirements of the Specific Plan other than
  design requirements, the Director must provide detailed written findings as to any
  inconsistency to the Applicant. The Applicant may revise and resubmit the application or
  appeal the Director’s decision as provided in Chapter VIII below.
  7. If the Director determines that an Individual Project is inconsistent, or is unable to
  determine consistency, with the design requirements of the Specific Plan, the Director
  may refer the matter to the Design Review Board or Planning Commission to consider in
  accordance with the design review provisions of the MPMC. The Design Review Board
  may make recommendations to the Planning Commission, or the Planning Commission
  may, on its own authority, determine consistency with the design requirements of the
  Specific Plan. The Applicant may revise and resubmit to the Director for reconsideration
  of any design found to be inconsistent or appeal the decision as provided in Chapter VIII
  below

 B.  DIRECTOR’S REVIEW
  The Director’s review and approval of a Project Clearance is an administrative clearance. The
  Director will act within 30 days after receiving an application for an Individual Project. If the
  Director fails to act within 30 days, the Individual Project is deemed approved. In approving a
  Project Clearance, the Director may impose conditions of approval as deemed necessary and
  those conditions of approval and SEIR mitigation measures set forth in Exhibit 1 that are
  applicable to the Individual Project. None of the actions by the Director under this Section VI are
  considered to be discretionary or require any CEQA review.

C.  ADVISORY DETERMINATION
  An Applicant may request, at the Applicant’s cost, that the Director conduct a preliminary review
  of an Individual Project application for an advisory non-binding determination of compliance with
  the provisions contained in this Specific Plan.

D.  RIGHTS GRANTED UNDER PROJECT CLEARANCE
  A Project Clearance indicates compliance with this Specific Plan and the Applicable Law.

E.  PROJECT CLEARANCE EXPIRATION
  A Project Clearance, including a design review consistency approval granted in accordance with
  the MPMC for an Individual Project, expires 36 months after the approval date unless within such
  period physical construction of the Individual Project is commenced and/or the beginning of the
  authorized use commenced, or the City grants a time extension in accordance with this Section.
  The Director may grant a one-year extension, for good cause shown, before the initial time period
  expires.

  VII. ADMINISTRATION OF SPECIFIC PLAN

A.  DIRECTOR AUTHORITY
  1. The Director may implement this Specific Plan in accordance with Applicable Law.
  2. The Director may interpret this Specific Plan. In the event that a specific use or type of use
  is not listed as a permitted use, the Director may determine whether the proposed use is
  similar to a permitted use and whether the use is permitted, permitted subject to
  conditions, permitted as a temporary use, or prohibited. In determining “similarity,” the
  Director must make all of the following findings:

  Page 317 of 410
   a. The proposed use meets the intent of, and is consistent with, the goals, objectives and
  policies of the general plan and the Specific Plan;
  b. The proposed use does not adversely impact the public health, safety, and general
  welfare of the City’s residents; and
  c. The proposed use shares characteristics common with, and is not of greater intensity
  or density or does not generate more environmental impacts than, those uses listed
  in the permitted uses section.

B.  AMENDMENTS
  1. This Specific Plan may be amended in the same manner as required for the adoption of
  Specific Plan.
  2. The following changes to a Specific Plan require a Specific Plan amendment:
  a. Changes to the text or maps other than (i) the addition of information that does not
  change the effect of any regulation, or (ii) changes to a Conceptual Plan that are in
  substantial conformance with the Specific Plan.
  b. Changes in any Specific Plan Area boundary.
  c. Increases in the specified density for the Specific Plan Area, except as expressly
  authorized under the Specific Plan.
  d. Increases in Trip Caps.
  e. Changes in standards or regulations, including landscaping and design standards,
  except to the extent the changes constitute a Minor Modification, as set forth in
  MPMC § 21.32.030.

C.  ADMINISTRATIVE MODIFICATIONS
  1. The Director is authorized to make technical corrections, in a form approved by the City
  Attorney, to maps, diagrams, tables, and other similar documents that may be required
  to reconcile the changes made by this Specific Plan and Applicable Law.
  2. In addition, the Director is authorized to make the following technical amendments, in a
  form approved by the City Attorney:
  a. Realignment or modifications to internal streets serving the project, lot lines,
  easement locations, and grading adjustments, if approved by the City Engineer.
  b. Minor modification to design criteria such as paving treatments, architectural details,
  and related criteria.
  c. Minor modification to landscape treatments, fencing, lighting, pedestrian paths, and
  entry treatments, provided the modifications are in substantial conformance with the

 1.  Introduction
1.1  PURPOSE OF MITIGATION MONITORING PROGRAM

This Mitigation Monitoring Program has been developed to provide a vehicle by which to monitor mitigation
measures and conditions of approval outlined in the 2000 Monterey Park Towne Plaza (MPTP) EIR, the
Supplemental Environmental Impact Report (Draft SEIR), and the Final Supplemental EIR (Final SEIR) (State
Clearinghouse No. 1999051058). The Mitigation Monitoring Program has been prepared in conformance with
Section 21081.6 of the Public Resources Code and City of Monterey Park Monitoring Requirements. Section
21081.6 states:

  (a) When making findings required by paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 21081 or
  when adopting a mitigated negative declaration pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision
  (c) of Section 21080, the following requirements shall apply:

  (1) The public agency shall adopt a reporting or monitoring program for the changes
  made to the project or conditions of project approval, adopted in order to mitigate or
  avoid significant effects on the environment. The reporting or monitoring program
  shall be designed to ensure compliance during project implementation. For those
  changes which have been required or incorporated into the project at the request of
  a responsible agency or a public agency having jurisdiction by law over natural
  resources affected by the project, that agency shall, if so requested by the lead or
  responsible agency, prepare and submit a proposed reporting or monitoring
  program.

  (2) The lead agency shall specify the location and custodian of the documents or other
  material which constitute the record of proceedings upon which its decision is
  based.

The Mitigation Monitoring Program will serve to document compliance with adopted/certified mitigation
measures, which are formulated to minimize impacts associated with the construction and operation of the
revised Monterey Park Market Place project (proposed project).

1.2  EIR SUMMARY

1.2.1  Previously Proposed 2000 Monterey Park Towne Plaza Site Plan

In March 2000, the Final EIR/EIS for the previous project was certified by the City of Monterey Park Planning
Commission. The City had the principal responsibility for project approval and acted as the CEQA lead
agency as defined by Section 15367 of the CEQA Guidelines. To help with the costs of land acquisition, site
cleanup, and required access, the City received a Section 108 Loan Guarantee and an accompanying
Economic Development Initiative grant from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).
Because of the assistance provided by HUD, the project was subject to National Environmental Protection Act
(NEPA) review, and HUD was the federal (NEPA) lead agency for the previous project.

The previous site plan required the demolition of all existing buildings, excluding the LTP, and the leveling of
the berm along SR-60 on the southern portion of the site. Contaminated berm soil (with traces of lead) would
be removed from the site while the remaining soil would be used to level the site. The previously proposed

garden centers, would make up a maximum of 561,011 square feet, nonanchor retail would make up 3,225 to

Although not included with the proposed project, a leachate treatment plant (LTP) and thermal destruction
facility (TDF) will continue to operate on the project site. Leachate is a common product of landfills, made of
groundwater and the compounds of decomposing material in the landfill. The LTP collects leachate from the
south parcel of the OII landfill and treats it. Off-gas is produced during leachate treatment and must be burned
in the treatment plant. The LTP directs off-gas to the South Parcel via a 12-inch pipeline, where it is burned
along with gas produced in the South Parcel. The TDF structure has two 60-foot high stacks, each
approximately 6 feet in diameter. It was constructed after the certification of the 2000 MPTP EIR and
improves the leachate treatment process. The structure would be contained by a chain-link fence and public
access would be restricted.

Monterey Park Market Place Precise Plan

The proposed project includes the Monterey Park Market Place (MPMP) Precise Plan, which is a required
document for development within the Regional-Specialty Center (R-S) Planned Development Overlay Zone to
ensure consistency with the Monterey Park General Plan. The purpose of having a precise plan is to describe
how the proposed project would meet the requirements of the Planned Development Overlay Zone on the
project site; provide the overall design concept for the site; implement the goals, policies, and objectives of
the City’s general plan as feasible; and establish the development regulations and framework for the project
site.

Detailed building and site development standards and regulations are included in the precise plan, such as
architectural themes, building height, and types of permitted businesses. Maximum height of buildings is set
in the MPMP Precise Plan and meets the standards of the R-S Planned Development Zone Overlay, which is
50 feet or 4 stories. Architectural features are allowed to project an additional 15 feet above maximum
building height with the approval of a conditional use permit. The proposed buildings would be between 30
and 50 feet in height (up to 60 feet with architectural features).

Project Access and Parking

The existing access road for the proposed project site is Greenwood Avenue, which enters the northern
boundary of the project site from Potrero Grande Drive. The main road through the development would be
named Market Place Drive. This road would be slightly realigned where it enters the project site on the north
and then extended toward the east corner of the site. Neil Armstrong Street would no longer intersect
Paramount Avenue but would intersect Market Place Drive instead. Market Place Drive would intersect
Paramount Avenue east of the project site. With the completion of all roadway improvements, the site would
be accessible from both Potrero Grande Drive and Paramount Boulevard off of SR-60.

Market Place Drive would serve as the main public/private roadway through the retail center and it would
allow truck and standard vehicle access. Additional specified truck/service routes would allow access to the
buildings to allow for pick-up and delivery of goods. The circulation plan for the project site will identify the
primary vehicle, truck/service, and pedestrian access routes on the project site.

Onsite parking is provided based on the parking demand ratio of the proposed land uses per 1,000 square
feet of building space, as shown in the far right column in Table 1. A minimum of 2,333 spaces would be
provided, including 44 handicapped spaces throughout the site, placed near the entrances for anchor stores,
the smaller mixed retail/restaurant stores, and the retail/restaurant pads. Although 2,333 are required, up to
2,386 would be provided, which would result in a surplus of up to 53 parking spaces. All parking lots are
aboveground surface lots and would be accessible from Market Place Drive.

Alternate Land Use Scenario: Small-Box Development

An alternative layout to the revised project is also provided for the project site in the event that the project
applicant opts to develop a small-box retail shopping center instead of the big-box retail. The small-box
alternative would have a reduced total square footage of 500,000 square feet that would include 3 anchors,
up to 10 smaller retail stores, and 7 retail pads. The retail anchor stores would line the northern boundary of
the project site and retail anchor “E” (110,000 square feet) would have a garden center (30,000 square feet).
The largest anchor, Retail A (140,000 square feet), would be north of the northern Greenwood Avenue
(Market Place Drive) entrance. South of Retail A, across Market Place Drive, are Retail stores G through M.
Retail F, which is adjacent to the LTP/TDF, Retail Pad 6, and Retail Pad 7 are all more centrally located on
the site and Retail B and C and Retail Pads 1 through 5 share the northern boundary of the site with the
anchor stores. Anchor stores would have a total square footage of 321,000, and retail nonanchor stores
would have a total square footage between 139,000 and 150,000, depending on whether Retail F is

1.3  PROJECT LOCATION

The proposed Monterey Park Market Place is in the southern portion of the City of Monterey Park and borders
the City of Montebello. It would be at 2550 Greenwood Avenue, north of SR-60 between the Paramount
Boulevard and Potrero Grande Drive freeway exits. The project site is bounded by Southern California Edison
(SCE) easements on the northwest and northeast. Beyond the SCE easements are Potrero Grande Drive to
the northwest and the Resurrection Cemetery and residential land uses to the northeast and east. Greenwood
Avenue accesses the site from the north from Potrero Grande Drive; Neil Armstrong Street intersects
Paramount Boulevard to the east of the site.

the State CEQA Guidelines (Section 15163, California Code of Regulations, Title 14, Division 6, Chapter 3).

avoid adverse effects.

1.4.3  Unavoidable Significant Adverse Impacts

With mitigation measures, air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, and transportation and traffic would have
significant and unavoidable impacts

Air Quality

Impact 5.2-2

Construction emissions exceed SCAQMD’s regional significance thresholds for NOx and would cumulatively
contribute to the SoCAB’s nonattainment designations. Grading emissions would be roughly the same
between the 2000 MPTP EIR and the revised MPMP Precise Plan. However, the 2000 MPTP EIR did not
identify significant construction emissions because construction activities were compared to screening
thresholds and were not modeled. SCAQMD now requires comparison to daily emissions thresholds and new
air pollutant models (e.g., URBEMIS) have been released to evaluate construction emissions. Modeling
results now show that even with implementation of Mitigation Measures 2-1 and 2-7, impacts from regional air
pollutant emissions from construction-related activities would exceed SCAQMD’s regional significance
thresholds for NOX as a result of use of heavy construction equipment. Mitigation Measure 2-7 would reduce
potentially significant impacts during Phase 1 construction activities to under the significance thresholds;
however, construction activities during Phase 2 site preparation would continue to exceed SCAQMD’s
regional significance thresholds for NOX. Therefore, impacts are significant and unavoidable. Regional
construction emissions impacts are a new significant unavoidable impact not identified in the 2000 MPTP EIR.

Impact 5.2-3

Operational phase emissions exceed SCAQMD’s regional significance thresholds for VOC, NOX, CO, PM10,
and PM2.5 and would cumulatively contribute to the SoCAB’s nonattainment designations. The MPMP Precise
Plan would exceed the thresholds for VOC, CO, NOX, PM10, and PM2.5. Mitigation Measures 2-8 through 2-17
would reduce operational emissions, to the extent feasible. Criteria air pollutant emissions that exceed
SCAQMD’s regional significance thresholds would cumulatively contribute to the NO 2, O3, and particulate
matter nonattainment designations of the SoCAB. While air quality impacts were identified in the 2000 MPTP
EIR, the MPMP Precise Plan would result in an approximately 5 to 8 percent increase in air quality impacts for
most criteria pollutants on weekdays and an approximately 44 percent increase in air quality impacts for most
criteria pollutants on weekends, compared to the 2000 MPTP. However, the project would result in a
decrease in air quality impacts based on emissions as identified in the 2000 MPTP EIR for CO (weekday
only), VOC, and NOx because of updated emission rates used in this SEIR that reflect lower emission rates
for vehicles. Further, based on the updated emission factors in the UREMIS2007 model, the revised SEIR
analysis has identified additional significant impacts associated with PM10 and PM2.5 that were not identified in
the EIR. The increase in air pollutant emissions would exceed the SCAQMD regional thresholds and therefore
the magnitude of change is considered to be significant. Modeling based on updated air pollutant emission
factors in the URBEMIS2007 model show that VOC, CO, NOX, PM10, and PM2.5 would exceed the significance
thresholds for the MPMP Precise Plan. Since emissions of particulate matter (PM 10 and PM2.5) were not

 2.  Mitigation Monitoring Process
2.1  MITIGATION MONITORING PROGRAM ORGANIZATION

CEQA requires that a reporting or monitoring program be adopted for the conditions of project approval that
are necessary to mitigate or avoid significant effects on the environment (Public Resources Code 21081.6).
The mitigation monitoring and reporting program is designed to ensure compliance with adopted mitigation
measures during project implementation. For each mitigation measure recommended in the Environmental
Impact Report, specifications are made herein that identify the action required and the monitoring that must
occur. In addition, a responsible agency is identified for verifying compliance with individual conditions of
approval contained in the Mitigation Monitoring Program (MMP). In order to effectively track and document
the status of mitigation measures, a mitigation matrix has been prepared and includes:

    Responsibility for implementation
    Timing
    Responsibility for monitoring
    Monitor

Mitigation measure timing of verification has been apportioned into several specific timing increments. Of
these, the most common are:

    Prior to project approval
    Prior to issuance of grading permit(s)
    During construction

Information pertaining to compliance with mitigation measures or any necessary modifications or refinements
will be documented in the comments portion of the matrix.

Supplement to the Certified 2000 EIR Mitigation Monitoring Program

Since this is a supplemental EIR, the MMP for this project modifies the previously adopted MMP for the
Monterey Park Towne Plaza (March 2000). The MMP for the SEIR includes the revised and new mitigation
measures for the proposed project. Where appropriate, the timing and responsible agency information from
the 2000 MMP has been retained.

2.2  MITIGATION MONITORING PROCEDURES

The City of Monterey Park Development Services Department is the designated lead agency for the Mitigation
Monitoring and Reporting Program. The City of Monterey Park includes the Mitigation Measures within the
Special Conditions of Approval. The City is responsible for review of all monitoring reports, enforcement
actions, and document disposition. The Community Development Department shall designate a Project
Mitigation Monitor for the proposed project.

 2. Mitigation Monitoring Process

2.2.1  In-Field Monitoring

The Responsible Monitoring Party shall exercise caution and professional practices at all times when
monitoring construction. Protective wear (hard hats, glasses, etc.) shall be worn at all times in construction
areas. Injuries shall be reported immediately to the Project Mitigation Monitor.

2.2.2  Coordination with Contractors

The construction manager/superintendent is responsible for coordination of contractors and for contractor
completion of required measures in accordance with the provisions of this program.

2.2.3  Recognized Experts

The use of recognized experts as a component of the monitoring team is required to ensure compliance with
scientific and engineering mitigation measures. While the recognized experts assess compliance with
required mitigation measures, consultation with the City of Monterey Park planning staff shall take place in the
event of a dispute.

2.2.4  Enforcement

Agencies may enforce conditions of approval through their existing police power, using stop-work orders,
fines, infraction citations, loss of entitlements, refusal to issue building permits or certificates of use and
occupancy or, in some cases, notice of violation for tax purposes. Criminal misdemeanor sanctions could be
available where the agency has adopted an ordinance requiring compliance with the monitoring program,
similar to the provision in many zoning ordinances that affirm the enforcement power to bring suit against
violators of the ordinances.

 3.  Mitigation Monitoring Requirements
3.1  CATEGORIZED MITIGATION MEASURES/MATRIX

Project-specific mitigation measures and project design features (PDFs) have been categorized in matrix
format, as shown in Table 3-1. The matrix identifies the environmental factor, specific mitigation measures,
schedule, and responsible monitor. The mitigation matrix will serve as the basis for scheduling the
implementation of, and compliance with, all mitigation measures.

A supplemental EIR only discusses new environmental impacts that would result from a change in the project
description between the original and revised projects and it only needs to contain the information necessary to
make the previous EIR adequate for the project as revised (CEQA Guidelines Section 15163). To avoid
certain environmental impacts, the City of Monterey Park has included certain PDFs, which are considered
part of the proposed project. The PDFs are mandatory and will be adopted by the City of Monterey Park as
part of the project’s conditions of approval. Both the PDFs and mitigation measures are part of the MMP to
be implemented by the City of Monterey Park. To provide a complete matrix that may be used for monitoring
and enforcement, this mitigation monitoring program includes mitigation measures and project design
features associated with the new impacts caused by the proposed project, as well as all mitigation measures
which remain effective from the previously certified 2000 MPTP EIR.

3.2  LONG-TERM MONITORING

Long-term monitoring related to several mitigation measures will be required, including fire safety inspections.
Postconstruction fire inspections are conducted on a routine basis by the City of Monterey Park Fire
Department.

 4.  Mitigation Monitoring Reports
Mitigation monitoring reports are required to document compliance with the Mitigation Monitoring Program
and to dispute arbitration enforcement resolution. Specific reports include:

    Field Check Report
    Implementation Compliance Report
    Arbitration/Enforcement Report

4.1  FIELD CHECK REPORT

Field check reports are required to record in-field compliance and conditions.

4.2  IMPLEMENTATION COMPLIANCE REPORT

The Implementation Compliance Report (ICR) is prepared to document the implementation of mitigation
measures on a phased basis, based on the information in Table 3-1. The report summarizes implementation
compliance, including mitigation measures, date completed, and monitor’s signature.

4.3  ARBITRATION/ENFORCEMENT REPORT

The Arbitration/Enforcement Report (AER) is prepared to document the outcome of arbitration committee
review and becomes a portion of the ICR.

  THE CITY COUNCIL DOES ORDAIN AS FOLLOWS:

SECTION 1. Recitals. The City Council finds and declares as follows:

  A. Monterey Park Retail Partners, LLC, a California Limited Liability Company
  (“Developer”) entered into a development agreement dated January 16, 2013
  (the “Development Agreement") with the City of Monterey Park (“City”), in
  connection with developing a commercial retail shopping center consisting of
  approximately 500,000 square feet and a minimum of 1,924 parking spaces on
  the Oil Cleanup/Edison site (the “Property”), as further described in the precise
  plan and tentative map approved in conjunction with the Development
  Agreement, known and referred to as the Monterey Park Market Place (the
  “Approved Project”).

  B. Developer and its affiliates propose to amend and restate the Development
  Agreement (the “Amended and Restated Development Agreement”) in
  connection with possible revisions to the Approved Project to allow the
  development of its final phase with retail, auto dealership, last mile distribution,
  and/or warehouse uses, parking, and related improvements, as further
  described in the specific plan (“Specific Plan”) being considered in conjunction
  with the Amended and Restated Development Agreement (the “Project”). The
  Amended and Restated Development Agreement is attached to this Ordinance
  as Exhibit “A,” and incorporated by reference.

  C. The City reviewed the Project’s environmental impacts under the California
  Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq., “CEQA”)
  and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 California Code of Regulations
  §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”).

  D. On June 7, 2023, the City Council conducted a duly noticed public hearing to
  consider the Amended and Restated Development Agreement. Notice of the
  time, place and purpose of the public hearing was duly provided in accordance
  with Government Code §§ 65867, 65090 and 65091 and Monterey Park
  Municipal Code (“MPMC”) § 21.32.070.

 Finding of Consistency with the Supplemental Environmental Impact Report for

  June 7, 2023

On September 16, 2021, Monterey Park Retail Partners Tract 3, LLC, submitted a request
for a conditional use permit (“CUP”) to add a fourth drive through restaurant at the Market
Place development that the City Council approved December 19, 2012 (the “Project”).
The Market Place Precise Plan allowed up to three drive-through restaurants be approved
ministerially; any subsequent drive-throughs require a CUP. The general layout, uses,
parking, and traffic patterns are all the same as originally contemplated by the City Council
on December 19, 2012.

The Project is considered a “project” under the California Environmental Quality Act
(“CEQA”). Accordingly, environmental review is required pursuant to CEQA (Public
Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq.) and the CEQA Guidelines (14 Cal. Code of
Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.).

Background

On December 19, 2012, the Monterey Park City Council adopted Resolution No. 11548
certifying the Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Report (SEIR) for the Market
Place project and adopting a Statement of Overriding Considerations (see Final EIR/EIS
at State Clearinghouse No. 1999051058). Implementation of mitigation measures
identified in the SEIR will be monitored as called for in the Mitigation Monitoring and
Reporting Program adopted on December 19, 2012.

The circumstances, impacts, and mitigation requirements identified in the SEIR remain
applicable to the proposed Project; there are no new issues and the level of environmental
impacts identified in the SEIR is static.

Environmental Analysis

CEQA Guidelines § 15168(c)(2) states that if a project is proposed which has been the
subject of a prior certified EIR, and “[i]f the [City] finds that pursuant to Section 15162, no
new effects could occur or new mitigation measures would be required, the agency can
approve the activity as being within the scope of the project covered by the … EIR, and
no new environmental document would be required.”
CEQA Guidelines § 15162 defines the conditions under which a subsequent EIR would
be required for a project as follows:
 (1)  Substantial changes are proposed in the project which require major revisions of
  the EIR due to the involvement of new significant environmental effects or

  Page 409 of 410
   substantial increase in the severity of previously identified significant effects;
 (2)  Substantial changes occur with respect to the circumstances under which the
  project is undertaken which will require major revisions of the previous EIR due to
  involvement of new significant environmental effects or a substantial increase in
  the severity of previously identified significant effects; and/or
 (3)  New information of substantial importance, which was not known and could not
  have been known with the exercise of reasonable diligence at the time the previous
  EIR was adopted, shows any of the following:
  1. The revised project will have one or more significant effects not discussed in
  the previous EIR;
  2. Significant effects previously examined will be substantially more severe than
  shown in the previous EIR;
  3. Mitigation measures or alternatives previously found not to be feasible would
  in fact be feasible and would substantially reduce one or more significant
  effects of the project, but the project proponents decline to adopt the mitigation
  measure or alternative; or
  4. Mitigation measures or alternatives which are considerably different from those
  analyzed in the previous EIR would substantially reduce one or more significant
  effects on the environment, but the project proponents decline to adopt the
  mitigation measure or alternative.

As stated above, the Project will not result in any new environmental effect not
already considered in the SEIR.

Findings

Based on the above analysis, the City Council of Monterey Park makes the following
findings:

1. On December 19, 2012, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 11548 and certified
  a Supplemental EIR for the project.
2. The Project will not facilitate the creation of any development beyond that anticipated
  and accounted for by the certified Supplemental EIR.
3. Approval of the Project will not result in any new or increased environmental effects,
  and no new mitigation measures are required.
4. Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines § 15168(c)(2), no new environmental documentation is
  required for approval of the Project.

1-A.  GEORGE ELDER MEMORIAL DAY

  The Monterey Park Police Department is celebrating the day of June 9th, as
  George Elder Memorial Day. This day is celebrated annually and honors Officer
  George Elder. Officer George Elder was only twenty-nine years old when he was
  shot and killed in the line of duty. Officer George Elder was in an exchange of
  gunfire while attempting to apprehend suspects who had just robbed a grocery
  store in Monterey Park. George Elder was transported to the hospital where he
  was pronounced dead. Three suspects were eventually convicted of first-degree
  murder. Officer George Elder was survived by his wife and three children. We are
  enlisting your support in the form of a resolution to honor Officer George Elder who
  was murdered protecting the residents of Monterey Park.

  Action Taken: The City Council adopted Resolution No. 2023-R44 declaring the

  On May 17, 2023, the City Council by a unanimous vote, continued the item to
  June 7, 2022.

  Program 15 of the Monterey Park Housing Element provides that the City Council
  will consider an inclusionary housing ordinance. The ordinance was originally
  presented to Council at its November 2, 2022 meeting, however the City Council
  recommended that a land dedication option be included in the ordinance, and
  referred the matter back to the Planning Commission for review.

  The Ordinance (Attachment 1, to the staff report) would encourage the production
  of affordable units in new housing developments. This is accomplished by several
  methods, or a combination of methods: (1) require actual construction of affordable
  units; (2) payment of an in-lieu fee to the City that commensurate with the cost of
  a the “affordability gap” between the market and affordable rate for the new unit or

  027, 029, 030, 031, 037, AND 038

  The Monterey Park Market Place development was originally approved through a
  Precise Plan (PP-12-01) that was intended to redevelop a brownfield site to help
  stimulate the local economy and create jobs while preserving the environment and
  public safety of the area. Since the creation and implementation of PP-12-01,
  Phase 1 is complete, but Phases 2 and 3 remains unbuilt. Phase 2 includes the
  wrap-around road south of the Leachate Treatment Plant (LTP) and Thermal
  Destruction Facility (TDF), and Phase 3 is the built-out of the area west of the
  LTP/TDF.

  In recent years, market forces changed the way in which consumers conduct
  business: a decreased need for traditional brick-and-mortar stores and an
  increased demand for last mile facilities, warehouses, auto dealerships, and sound
  stages for the entertainment industry emerged since the beginning of the COVID-
  19 pandemic. The applicant seeks to create flexibility to allow for land uses that
  help address the changing landscape of the commercial/service sector by
  providing a framework through the proposed Market Place Specific Plan (“MPSP”)
  to allow for such uses. No immediate construction or development is proposed at
  this time.

  The Project includes the proposed adoption of the MPSP to address the eventual
  build-out of the Market Place; it supersedes the existing Precise Plan. The Specific
  Plan will be identified within the Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) and the
  entire Market Place Project site will be re-zoned from the Regional Specialty
  Center with Planned Development Overlay, to the MPSP. Further, the amended
  and restated Development agreement between the City and the Applicant will help
  ensure that the eventual build-out of the Market Place will provide a public benefit
  to the community.

  Most recently, the City Council considered a similar proposal of the site that was
  not approved at its April 19, 2023 meeting. Following that date, on May 15, 2023,
  the applicant submitted a new application. That application includes a revised
  Specific Plan that includes new uses that would be permitted at the site for
  additional Council consideration.
